Beneath enormous surface variety, he claimed, the tales are built from a fixed inventory of thirty-one functions, where a function is an act defined by its significance for the course of the action rather than by who performs it or how. Absentation, interdiction, violation, reconnaissance, trickery, villainy or lack, departure, testing, receipt of a magical agent, struggle, branding, victory, return, pursuit, rescue, unrecognised arrival, difficult task, recognition, exposure, transfiguration, punishment, wedding. Not every tale uses all of them, but those that appear, Propp argued, always appear in the same order. He paired this with seven roles, or spheres of action: villain, donor, helper, princess and her father, dispatcher, hero and false hero. A role is not a person. One character can occupy several roles and one role can be spread over several characters, which is why a horse, a hag in a hut and a dead father can all be donors. The abstraction is the point: it lets you see that a Bond film, a fairy tale and a recruitment story about a graduate joining a firm can share a skeleton while sharing nothing else. Propp's method fed directly into French structuralism after his book was translated into English in 1958. A. J. Greimas compressed the seven roles into six actants arranged in three oppositions: subject and object, sender and receiver, helper and opponent. Claude Bremond built a model of narrative as a branching tree of triads, each an opportunity that is either taken or missed and then either succeeds or fails, which captures something Propp's linear list does not, namely that at every point the story could have gone otherwise. Joseph Campbell's monomyth or hero's journey, from The Hero with a Thousand Faces in 1949, belongs to the same family but was arrived at through comparative mythology and Jungian psychology rather than formal analysis, and it is considerably less rigorous. The critique is worth taking seriously. Propp's corpus was narrow, a single genre in a single language, and the functions are elastic enough that a determined analyst can fit almost anything into them, which makes the scheme hard to falsify. Applied carelessly to modern fiction it flattens exactly what is interesting. Campbell's version has done real damage in screenwriting culture, where it is often deployed as a template to be filled rather than a pattern occasionally observed. The defensible use is diagnostic rather than generative: the models are good at showing what a story has in common with others, which is precisely the information a writer needs in order to depart from it deliberately.

sections.heading: Narrative Time: Order, Duration and Frequency
sections.body: Gerard Genette's Discours du recit, published in 1972 as part of Figures III and translated as Narrative Discourse, gives the most complete analysis of narrative time available, developed through a book-length reading of Proust. He separates three independent variables, and keeping them separate resolves a great deal of muddle. Order concerns the relation between the sequence of events and the sequence of the telling. Any departure is an anachrony. An analepsis reaches back to something earlier, what film calls a flashback; a prolepsis reaches forward, a flash-forward. Genette further asks about reach, how far from the present moment the anachrony goes, and extent, how much time it covers, and whether it is external, falling entirely outside the main span, internal, falling inside it, or mixed. The opening of Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, in which a colonel facing a firing squad remembers a distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice, executes a prolepsis and an analepsis in a single sentence and announces the novel's whole temporal method. Duration concerns speed: the ratio between how long events take and how much text is spent on them. Five values cover the field. Ellipsis spends no text on an interval, and the phrase three years passed is a whole decade of narrative machinery in three words. Summary compresses, a paragraph for a season. Scene runs at roughly parity, which in practice means dialogue. Stretch spends more text than the event takes, common in moments of violence or revelation where a half-second gets a page. Pause spends text while narrative time stops entirely, as in a description of a room or an essayistic digression. Rhythm in fiction is largely the pattern of these five, and manuscripts that feel monotonous are usually stuck in one of them, typically unbroken scene. Frequency concerns how many tellings correspond to how many occurrences. Singulative narration tells once what happened once. Repeating narration tells several times what happened once, the method of Rashomon and of much modernist fiction. Iterative narration tells once what happened many times, and signals itself with words like every Sunday or he would always. Proust is the great iterative writer, and Genette showed that his pseudo-iterative passages, which describe with impossible specificity a scene supposedly typical of many, are a distinctive and slightly illogical effect. The practical value is diagnostic precision. When a draft drags, the problem is nearly always duration: scenes are running at parity where summary would do. When a structure feels confusing rather than intriguing, the problem is usually order: too many anachronies without clear signposting of which present the reader should treat as home. Naming the variable makes the fix obvious.

sections.heading: Voice: Who Speaks, and From Where
sections.body: Genette's second great clarification was to insist that the question who speaks is entirely separate from the question who sees. Conflating them is the single most common error in ordinary talk about point of view, and it is why the school phrase third-person limited omniscient causes so much confusion. Voice is the speaking instance: the narrator, whose properties can be catalogued along three axes. The first axis is person, or more precisely the narrator's relation to the story. A homodiegetic narrator is a character within the world being narrated; if that narrator is also the protagonist, Genette calls the case autodiegetic, as with David Copperfield or Huckleberry Finn. A heterodiegetic narrator is absent from the story world, the standard third-person case. What matters is not the pronoun but the membership: Nick Carraway in The Great Gatsby narrates in the first person about someone else, which is homodiegetic but not autodiegetic, and that marginal position is exactly what the novel exploits. Second-person narration, as in Italo Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveller or Jay McInerney's Bright Lights, Big City, is rarer and tends to foreground the act of address itself. The second axis is level. An extradiegetic narrator sits outside any narrated frame and addresses the reader directly. An intradiegetic narrator is a character inside a story who tells another story, as Scheherazade does in the Thousand and One Nights, and characters inside her tales who tell further tales are metadiegetic. Frame structures of this kind are ancient and durable; Chaucer, Boccaccio, Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and Wuthering Heights all use them, usually to raise a question about transmission and trust. The third axis is time of narration. Subsequent narration, the overwhelming default, tells of events already complete, which grants hindsight, retrospective irony and the ability to say he did not yet know. Simultaneous narration runs in the present tense alongside the action, buying immediacy at the cost of perspective. Prior narration is predictive or prophetic and is rare outside scripture. Interpolated narration alternates, and is the natural mode of epistolary and diary fiction, where a letter is written between events and the writer's ignorance of what comes next is dramatically useful. Distinct from all this is distance: how audible the narrator is. A narrator can be effaced almost to transparency, as in much of Hemingway, or intrusive to the point of becoming the main attraction, as in Fielding's Tom Jones or the essayistic asides of George Eliot's Middlemarch. Twentieth-century Anglophone teaching, following Henry James and Percy Lubbock, hardened a preference for effacement into a rule, show don't tell, which is a stylistic fashion of a particular period rather than a law and has cost a great many novels their best sentences.

sections.heading: Focalization: Who Sees, and How Much They Know
sections.body: Focalization is the regulation of information: the filter through which the narrated world reaches the reader. Genette introduced the term in 1972 precisely to break the old habit of describing perspective in optical metaphors like point of view, which smuggle in the assumption that perceiving and speaking are the same act. They are not. A narrator can speak from outside while restricting what is shown to what a single character could perceive, and that combination is the workhorse of the modern novel. Genette proposed three degrees. Zero focalization, loosely called omniscience, means the narrative is not restricted to any single consciousness: it can enter any mind, move to any place, and know outcomes in advance. Fielding, Tolstoy and George Eliot work this way, and it permits comparative moral judgement across a whole society, which is why the nineteenth-century social novel needed it. Internal focalization restricts perception to one character's field. It may be fixed on one character throughout, as in Henry James's What Maisie Knew, variable, shifting between characters in different sections as in Woolf's Mrs Dalloway, or multiple, presenting the same event through several filters in turn. External focalization stays outside every consciousness, reporting only what a camera and a microphone would catch, refusing all interiority. Hemingway's Hills Like White Elephants is the standard demonstration: two people drink and talk for a few pages, no thought is ever reported, and the reader must infer a pregnancy and an argument about abortion from word choice alone. The formula that makes the concept usable is a comparison of knowledge. In zero focalization the narrative knows more than any character. In internal focalization it knows exactly what the focal character knows. In external focalization it knows less. That comparison is the lever behind almost every effect of suspense and irony. Give the reader more than the character and you get dread; give the character more than the reader and you get mystery; keep them level and you get identification. Two refinements matter in practice. First, focalization can shift, and unmarked shifts are the technical fault often called head-hopping: a paragraph anchored in one mind that suddenly reports another character's private thought, breaking the contract without announcing it. The problem is not the shift but the absence of a signal, which is why a section break does the job that a comma cannot. Second, focalization is not only perceptual. Mieke Bal, whose 1985 Narratology developed the concept further, noted that a filter carries ideological and emotional colouring too: the focalizer's values determine which details in a room are worth mentioning, and a description is therefore always a characterisation of the describer. A soldier, an estate agent and a child walk into the same house and three genuinely different rooms appear on the page.

sections.heading: Free Indirect Discourse and the Rendering of Consciousness
sections.body: The representation of what goes on inside a mind is the technical problem the novel spent two centuries solving, and the solution that mattered most is free indirect discourse, known in French as style indirect libre and in German as erlebte Rede. It works by fusing a narrator's grammar with a character's idiom. Direct discourse gives the words in quotation marks with a tag: She thought, I must leave tomorrow. Indirect discourse subordinates them: She thought that she must leave the next day. Free indirect discourse drops both the tag and the subordination while keeping the narrator's third person and past tense: She must leave tomorrow. There was nothing else for it. The effect is a genuine merger of two voices that cannot be cleanly separated, and that ambiguity is the whole point. The reader hears the character's diction, exclamations and self-justifications while the narrator's frame remains lightly present, so the same sentence can convey a thought and quietly appraise it. Jane Austen is the technique's first great master; the opening of Emma, describing a heroine who seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence and had lived nearly twenty-one years with very little to distress or vex her, is affectionate and faintly ironic at once, and the irony lives in the gap between the character's self-assessment and the narrator's phrasing of it. Flaubert made the method systematic in Madame Bovary in 1857, where the sentimental clichés of Emma's inner life are given in her own register while the surrounding prose declines to endorse them. Joyce, Woolf and Kafka took it further, and much contemporary literary fiction now uses it as the default mode without naming it. Stream of consciousness is a related but distinct thing, and the two are routinely confused. Free indirect discourse is a grammatical technique; stream of consciousness is an ambition, the attempt to render the associative flow of a mind including its incoherence. Interior monologue is one means to that end, quoting the mind's language directly, unmediated and often unpunctuated, as in Molly Bloom's closing chapter of Ulysses. Psycho-narration, Dorrit Cohn's term from her 1978 study Transparent Minds, is the opposite pole: the narrator describes a character's mental state in the narrator's own vocabulary, including states the character could not articulate. All three coexist in most serious novels, often within a single paragraph. The trade-off is precise and worth stating. Free indirect discourse buys intimacy without surrendering control, but it makes reliability harder to locate, since a false statement in the fused voice may be the character's error or the narrator's assertion, and the text may offer no way to decide. Skilful writers exploit that undecidability. Careless ones produce prose where the reader cannot tell whether a judgement is being made or merely reported, which reads as muddle rather than as subtlety.

sections.heading: Character: Function, Trait, and the Illusion of Persons
sections.body: Narratology approaches character with a productive discomfort. Readers experience characters as people, argue about their motives and mourn them; the theory insists they are made of words, exist only where the text puts them, and have no properties beyond those the text supplies or a reader infers. Both things are true, and the useful question is how a pattern of marks on paper reliably produces the experience of encountering a person. The structuralist answer, running from Propp through Greimas, treats character as function: an actant defined by its position in the action rather than by any inner life. This is unglamorous and genuinely powerful for analysing plot-driven forms, where a helper is whatever helps. The mimetic answer, most fully argued by James Phelan, holds that characters have three simultaneous dimensions. The mimetic is their aspect as possible persons, which supports empathy and moral judgement. The thematic is their aspect as representatives of ideas or groups, which supports interpretation. The synthetic is their aspect as artificial constructs, which is normally suppressed but can be foregrounded, as in metafiction where a character discovers she is in a book. Different genres weight these differently: allegory is thematically dominant, realist fiction mimetically dominant, and much postmodern fiction deliberately pushes the synthetic dimension forward. Characterisation itself operates by a small set of channels. Direct definition states a trait outright, which is efficient and low-credibility because readers discount assertion. Indirect presentation shows behaviour, speech, thought, appearance and environment and lets the reader infer, which is slower and far more convincing, and is the real content of the advice to show rather than tell. Analogy works by placement: a character who is repeatedly described near a caged bird, or whose name is Sharp, acquires a colouring the text never asserts. Contrast between characters does an enormous amount of quiet work, which is why a foil is often the cheapest way to make a protagonist legible. Naming is a channel in its own right: Dickens gets a third of his characterisation done before a figure has spoken, and the reason Gradgrind and Micawber work is that English sound symbolism is doing unpaid labour. E. M. Forster's 1927 distinction between flat and round characters remains useful if held loosely. A flat character is built round a single idea and can be summarised in a sentence; a round character is capable of surprising the reader convincingly. Forster did not think flat characters were failures. They are the right tool for comedy, for large casts, and for anyone whose job in the story is to be reliably themselves. The genuine failure is a character whose surprises are not convincing, meaning the text has not laid down the material that makes the surprise legible in retrospect. That is a construction problem, not a depth problem: consistency is not the requirement, retrospective intelligibility is.

sections.heading: Storyworld, Setting and the Logic of Fictional Worlds
sections.body: A narrative does not merely report events; it invites a reader to build a world in which those events can be located. Postclassical theorists call the mental model the reader constructs the storyworld, and the shift of emphasis from text to model is one of the more useful developments of the last thirty years. It explains a fact that older theory struggled with: readers routinely know things about a story that the text never states. Nobody is told that a nineteenth-century London street has a sky, but everyone imagines one, because comprehension proceeds by importing the actual world wholesale and then applying only the deviations the text specifies. Marie-Laure Ryan named this the principle of minimal departure, and it is the reason a fantasy novel need only tell you that dragons exist, not that gravity still does. Setting therefore does more than provide scenery. It carries at least four loads. It supplies plausibility constraints, which is why a locked-room mystery must establish the geometry of the room before the body appears. It generates obstacles, so that a desert, a border or a class system is a machine for producing plot. It functions expressively, colouring events by association, an operation the nineteenth century overworked into the pathetic fallacy where weather agrees with feeling. And it encodes ideology, since the choice of which spaces are shown and which are unmarked backdrop reveals whose experience the narrative treats as normal. The formal study of fictional worlds borrows from modal logic. Lubomir Dolezel and Ryan describe a storyworld as a system with a factual domain, what is true in it, surrounded by satellite domains: what characters believe, wish, fear, intend and pretend. Conflict, on this account, is a mismatch between domains, and plot is the process by which the mismatches are resolved or destroy someone. The framework handles genre elegantly. Realist fiction keeps the physical laws of the actual world and varies only particulars. Fantasy alters those laws but demands internal consistency, which is why a magic system with no stated costs feels weightless. Science fiction alters them with an implied causal explanation, the device Darko Suvin called the novum. Impossible worlds, in Borges or Alain Robbe-Grillet, deliberately contain contradictions that cannot be reconciled, and the reader's failure to build a stable model is the intended experience rather than a fault. The practical rule that follows is about the placement of information. A constraint that will later matter must be established before it is needed, or the resolution reads as invention on demand, the fault usually called a deus ex machina after the crane that lowered gods onto the Greek stage. Establishing it too obtrusively, however, telegraphs the outcome. The craft solution is to introduce load-bearing facts while the reader's attention is on something else, which is why Chekhov's gun on the wall is usually hung during an argument about something entirely different.

sections.heading: Frames, Embedded Tales and Metalepsis
sections.body: Narratives nest. A novel can contain a letter that contains a memory that contains a joke, and each enclosure creates a new level with its own teller and audience. Genette's terminology is worth learning because the alternatives are vague: the outermost telling is extradiegetic, the world it narrates is the diegetic level, a story told by a character inside that world produces a metadiegetic level, and so on downward. The nesting can in principle be indefinite, and the Thousand and One Nights reaches four or five levels in places. Embedded narratives are not ornament; they do specific work. They motivate transmission, answering the question of how this account reached us, which matters greatly in horror and in testimony-based fiction. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein of 1818 wraps the creature's account inside Victor's account inside Walton's letters to his sister, so that every claim arrives thrice mediated and the reader is never given unfiltered access to the most contested testimony in the book. They also permit contrast, since an inset tale can rhyme with or invert the frame, and they allow a text to display interpretation happening: in Conrad's Heart of Darkness the listeners on the Nellie are visible, and their silences are part of the meaning. The most interesting phenomenon at these boundaries is metalepsis, Genette's term for an illegitimate crossing between levels. A narrator addressing a character, a character reading the book she is in, an author appearing in his own fiction to argue with a creation: each violates the logical separation the frame set up. Metalepsis can be a joke, as when Sterne asks the reader to help him lift Uncle Toby, or vertiginous, as in Julio Cortazar's story Continuity of Parks, where a man reading a novel about a murderer is killed by the murderer he is reading about. Its power depends entirely on the boundary having felt solid first, which is why metafiction wears out fast in cultures already saturated with it. Two related structures deserve names. Mise en abyme is an embedded miniature that reproduces the shape of the whole work, the play within Hamlet being the standard case; the term comes from heraldry, where a shield can carry a smaller image of itself. The unreliable frame is the case where a frame narrator's own motives call the embedded story into question, so that the reader must weigh not just the tale but the teller's reason for telling it. The design caution is simple and often ignored. Each level added costs the reader working memory and puts distance between them and the innermost events. That distance is exactly the point when the theme is transmission, testimony or the unreliability of accounts, and it is dead weight otherwise. A frame that never returns, or that exists only to explain how a manuscript was found, is usually a first-chapter habit inherited from the eighteenth century rather than a structural decision.

sections.heading: Reliability, the Implied Author, and Reading Against the Text
sections.body: Wayne C. Booth, in The Rhetoric of Fiction of 1961, introduced two ideas that have organised argument ever since. The first is the implied author: not the historical person who wrote the book, and not the narrator, but the picture of an authorial intelligence a reader constructs from the text's total design, including its ironies and its silences. The second, defined in terms of the first, is unreliable narration. A narrator is unreliable when the reader has grounds to believe that his account diverges from the norms and facts the implied author endorses. The definition matters because unreliability is not lying. A narrator who deliberately deceives is one case, but the richer cases involve narrators who report honestly and misjudge. Phelan usefully splits unreliability along three axes. A narrator may misreport, getting facts wrong; misread, interpreting events incorrectly; or misregard, applying values the text does not share. Huckleberry Finn misregards constantly, believing he is damned for helping Jim escape, and the whole moral force of the novel lies in the reader's ability to see past his ethics to Twain's. Stevens in Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day of 1989 misreads a life, and the reader assembles from his evasions a story of wasted love and complicity with fascism that the butler never quite tells. Nabokov's Humbert Humbert misreports and misregards while writing gorgeously, which is precisely the trap the prose sets. The signals of unreliability are technical and learnable. Internal contradiction, where the account does not square with itself. Verifiable error, where a claim conflicts with something the text has established. Excessive protestation, where a narrator argues for his own fairness at length. Conspicuous gaps at emotionally loaded moments. Style that betrays the speaker, as when a childlike vocabulary persists through adult material. Corroboration failure, where other characters behave in ways that make sense only if the narrator is wrong. Readers detect these largely without noticing, which is why unreliable narration produces the peculiar pleasure of feeling clever. The concept has a real critical difficulty, worth admitting rather than smoothing over. Locating the implied author's norms requires interpretation, so unreliability can become a device for dismissing any narrator whose values a critic dislikes, and Ansgar Nunning and others have argued that the concept smuggles the reader's own frame in under the guise of textual evidence. The cognitive reframing is more defensible: unreliability is what happens when a reader cannot reconcile a narrator's account with the inferences the text otherwise supports, and so builds a second model running underneath the first. That is a description of a mental event rather than a property of ink, and it has the advantage of explaining why the same novel reads as unreliable to one generation and straightforward to another.

sections.heading: Narrative Beyond the Page: Film, Drama, Comics and Games
sections.body: The machinery described so far was mostly derived from novels, and one of the strongest tests of narratology is whether it transfers. Largely it does, but each medium supplies its own resources and imposes its own constraints, and the differences are instructive. Film has no narrator by default; it has a camera, and the camera focalizes without speaking. Perspective is achieved by shot selection, and the point-of-view shot, the eyeline match and the shot-reverse-shot pattern do the work that pronouns do in prose. Interiority is film's expensive problem, solved by voiceover, by performance, or by the Kuleshov effect, the demonstration attributed to Lev Kuleshov around 1918 that an identical neutral face intercut with soup, a coffin or a woman is read as hunger, grief or desire. That finding is really a claim about narrative comprehension in general: meaning is assembled at the join, not delivered in the shot. Editing controls duration precisely, and the cut is film's ellipsis. Drama in performance has no narrator either, and everything must be externalised into speech, action and stage image; the soliloquy is a technology invented to solve the interiority problem, and the chorus and the raisonneur are others. Comics narrate through a spatial arrangement in which the reader controls pacing, and Scott McCloud's 1993 Understanding Comics showed that the gutter between panels is where closure happens: the reader supplies the connecting action, and a panel transition from moment to moment, action to action, scene to scene or aspect to aspect determines how much they must supply. Digital games raise the sharpest theoretical question, because the audience acts. The ludology versus narratology dispute of roughly 1999 to 2005, associated with Espen Aarseth, Gonzalo Frasca and Janet Murray, produced heat and eventually a workable settlement: games contain narrative material but are not reducible to it, and their distinctive contribution is that a player's actions generate part of the fabula. Useful vocabulary followed. Embedded narrative is authored in advance and encountered; emergent narrative arises from the interaction of systems and is not authored at all. Environmental storytelling, Henry Jenkins's term, distributes story information through space rather than time, so that a ransacked room is a narrative event a player reconstructs. The unresolved tension, sometimes called ludonarrative dissonance after Clint Hocking's 2007 essay, is between what a story says a character is and what the mechanics let a player do. Oral narrative deserves a mention because it is the oldest form and the one most people practise daily. William Labov's sociolinguistic work in the late 1960s on spontaneous personal narratives found a recurring six-part shape: abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution and coda. The evaluation clause, the moment where a teller signals why the story is worth hearing, is the part inexperienced storytellers omit, and its absence is the reason an anecdote lands as so what.

sections.heading: Cognitive and Rhetorical Turns: Narrative as Transaction
sections.body: Since roughly 1990 the centre of gravity has moved from cataloguing textual features to explaining what happens in a reader's mind and what a narrative is doing between people. Two overlapping programmes dominate. Cognitive narratology, associated with David Herman, Monika Fludernik, Manfred Jahn and Lisa Zunshine, treats narrative comprehension as ordinary cognition working on unusual material. Its central claims are testable and mostly hold up. Readers build and update a situation model, a mental representation of who is where, wanting what, which is why an unexplained change of location is disorienting and why a paragraph that establishes a spatial frame is easier to follow. Readers apply scripts, stored expectations about routine sequences such as visiting a restaurant, and narrative interest lives largely in script violation. Readers run theory of mind continuously, attributing beliefs and intentions to characters, and Zunshine argues that fiction is attractive partly because it exercises this faculty at higher embedding depths than daily life offers. Fludernik's provocative thesis in Towards a Natural Narratology of 1996 is that narrativity itself is grounded not in plot but in experientiality, the sense of a human consciousness undergoing something, which explains why a plotless story about a person noticing a room still reads as a narrative while a plot summary does not. Rhetorical narratology, developed by Booth's successors and most systematically by James Phelan, defines narrative as somebody telling somebody else on some occasion and for some purpose that something happened. Every term in that formula is a variable, and analysis consists of tracking how the four dimensions interact. Its strength is that it restores intention and effect without naive biographical criticism, and it handles ethics natively: a narrative makes claims on a reader's judgement, invites certain sympathies and forecloses others, and that invitation can be examined. Alongside these sit critical extensions that ask whose stories the classical models were built from. Feminist narratology, launched by Susan Lanser's 1986 essay Toward a Feminist Narratology, showed that categories like public and private narration carry gendered histories and that authority in narration has never been evenly distributed. Postcolonial and queer narratology make parallel arguments about whose plots count as complete, noting that the marriage plot and the bildungsroman encode particular life courses as normal. These are not decorations on the formal system; they are claims that the formal system was generalised from an unrepresentative sample, which is a methodological point of exactly the kind narratology should take seriously. The honest summary is that no single framework now commands the field. Classical structural description remains the best tool for saying what a text does; cognitive work explains why it lands; rhetorical work explains what it is for; critical extensions ask who it serves. A competent analyst uses all four and does not pretend the seams are invisible.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and What To Do When a Story Will Not Work
sections.body: Most narrative failures are structural rather than sentence-level, and most reduce to a small number of diagnosable faults. Knowing them by name turns a vague sense that something is wrong into a repair. The commonest is a missing want. If no one in a scene is trying to get something, the scene has no shape and readers experience it as drift, however good the prose. The second is an absent or costless obstacle, which produces a sequence of events in which nothing is risked; the symptom is that a summary of the chapter sounds like a list. The third is flat stakes: things go wrong at a constant severity, so the tenth setback carries the weight of the first. The fourth is a resolution the reader could not have anticipated but also cannot accept in retrospect, the deus ex machina, whose cure is not to remove the surprise but to plant its conditions earlier and inconspicuously. The fifth is coincidence used to solve rather than to complicate; the working rule is that coincidence may create a problem and may not resolve one. The sixth is a pacing fault, almost always excess scene where summary belongs, detectable by asking how many minutes of story time a page covers and whether that ratio ever changes. Perspective faults form their own family. Unsignalled focalization shifts read as carelessness rather than range. A first-person narrator who reports facts he could not know breaks the contract quietly and permanently. A narrator whose voice does not vary with mood or circumstance flattens a whole book. And an unreliable narrator with no accessible counter-evidence is not unreliable; he is simply the text, since unreliability requires a second signal the reader can triangulate against. There are also genuine limits to what this analysis can do, and pretending otherwise wastes people's time. Structural soundness does not produce interest: a perfectly built plot about nothing anyone cares about remains inert. The models generalise from particular traditions, mostly European prose fiction of the last three centuries, and applied to oral epic, to Noh drama, to Aboriginal songline narrative or to serialised soap opera they distort as much as they reveal. And structural analysis is retrospective by nature, which is why it diagnoses well and generates badly; every attempt to turn narratology into a writing formula, from the strict Proppian template to the fifteen-beat commercial screenplay sheet, has produced competent, forgettable work. The practical procedure when a draft is not working is therefore diagnostic and ordered. Reconstruct the fabula in plain sentences and see whether it is interesting when stripped of style. Mark the causal links and find where and follows and rather than because. Check whether the focal character wants something in every scene and whether failing to get it costs anything. Time the durations. Only then consider voice and sentence. Nine times in ten, the fault is upstream of the prose the writer has been polishing.

guides.title: Genre Theory & the Classification of Literature
guides.summary: A comprehensive account of how literature is sorted into kinds: the classical and Romantic systems, the structuralist and cognitive turns, how genres actually form and change, the major branches of modern genre thinking, and the practical uses and recurring failures of literary classification.

sections.heading: What Genre Is and Why Classification Is Unavoidable
sections.body:
Genre, from the French for kind or sort, and ultimately from the Latin genus, is the practice of sorting texts into groups on the basis of shared features, and the body of thought about how and why that sorting works. It looks at first like a librarian's problem — a matter of shelving — and it turns out to be one of the most theoretically loaded questions in the study of literature, because how a text is classified determines how it is read, what is expected of it, what counts as a fault in it, and often whether it is taken seriously at all.

The reason classification cannot simply be abandoned is that reading is impossible without it. No reader approaches a text without expectations. Encountering the opening "Once upon a time" activates a set of assumptions about what will follow: talking animals will not be a defect, a happy resolution is likely, psychological realism is not required, and asking which century the story takes place in is a category error. Encountering "The defendant entered a plea of not guilty on 14 March" activates entirely different expectations. Neither response is optional or deliberate; the classification is made in the first few words and everything afterward is processed through it. E. D. Hirsch made the point sharply in 1967 when he argued that all understanding of verbal meaning is necessarily genre-bound, because the meaning of any utterance depends on the kind of utterance it is taken to be.

This is why genre is often described as a contract or a set of instructions rather than a container. The eighteenth-century reader who opened a novel purporting to be a discovered manuscript, and the modern reader who opens a memoir, are both entering an agreement about what claims are being made and what kind of scrutiny is appropriate. Violations of that agreement — a memoir found to be invented, a documentary found to be staged — provoke a distinctive kind of anger that has nothing to do with the quality of the writing and everything to do with the broken contract.

Genre also has a productive side that is easy to miss when it is described only as a constraint. Writers do not merely obey genre conventions; they use them as a resource. The conventions supply a shorthand that lets a story get moving without explaining everything, and they supply a set of expectations that can be gratified, delayed, subverted or refused. A large proportion of literary effect depends on the reader's genre knowledge, because surprise requires an expectation to violate. The sonnet's fourteen lines are not a cage but a pressure vessel; the detective story's guarantee of a solution is what makes the middle of the book suspenseful rather than merely confusing.

The hard question, which the rest of any serious treatment must confront, is whether genres are real things with definable boundaries or convenient fictions imposed after the fact. The answer that has emerged over two millennia is neither simple yes nor simple no.

sections.heading: The Classical System: Aristotle, Horace and the Three Kinds
sections.body:
Western genre theory begins with Aristotle's Poetics, written around 335 BCE and surviving in a damaged single book, with the promised second book on comedy lost. Its influence is out of all proportion to its length, and much of what later ages took from it was distortion.

Aristotle's organising principle is mimesis, imitation or representation. All poetry imitates, and kinds of poetry are distinguished by three variables: the medium of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony, in various combinations), the objects imitated (people better than us, worse than us, or like us), and the manner (narration versus dramatic enactment). Tragedy imitates people better than ourselves in dramatic manner; comedy imitates people worse; epic imitates the elevated in narrative manner. This is a genuinely analytic scheme, generating kinds from a small set of parameters rather than merely listing them.

His account of tragedy supplies the most-quoted definitions in criticism. Tragedy is the imitation of an action that is serious, complete and of a certain magnitude, in language embellished with artistic ornament, in dramatic rather than narrative form, effecting through pity and fear the catharsis of such emotions. The meaning of catharsis — purgation, purification, clarification, or something else — has been argued about continuously for 2,300 years without resolution, which is itself instructive about how much interpretive weight a single Greek noun can be made to bear. Aristotle further specifies six components in order of importance: plot, character, thought, diction, melody and spectacle, with plot first because tragedy imitates action rather than persons. He introduces hamartia, usually mistranslated as "tragic flaw" but better rendered as an error or mistake, often of ignorance rather than character; peripeteia, the reversal; and anagnorisis, the recognition.

Horace's Ars Poetica, composed around 19 BCE as a verse letter, added the prescriptive dimension that dominated later reception. Its themes are decorum and consistency: each genre has its proper metre, subject and diction, and mixing them produces the absurdity of his opening image, a human head grafted onto a horse's neck. He supplies the formula that poetry should be both dulce and utile, sweet and useful, and the advice to begin in medias res.

The Renaissance and neoclassical periods hardened these observations into rules. Julius Caesar Scaliger's Poetices libri septem (1561) and Nicolas Boileau's L'Art poétique (1674) codified a hierarchy of genres with epic and tragedy at the summit and pastoral, satire and lyric below. The three unities of action, time and place, often attributed to Aristotle, are largely the invention of the Italian critic Lodovico Castelvetro in 1570; Aristotle mentions unity of action, remarks in passing on the length of a tragedy, and says nothing prescriptive about place. This misattribution shaped French classical drama for a century and provoked the reaction that followed.

sections.heading: The Romantic Revolt and the Historicising of Kinds
sections.body:
The neoclassical system was attacked in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries from two directions at once, and the attack changed what genre could mean.

The first line of attack was empirical: Shakespeare. English drama mixed tragedy and comedy, changed location freely, spanned years, and put clowns in the middle of catastrophes, and it was manifestly great. Samuel Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765) argued directly that the unities were not necessary to dramatic pleasure because audiences were never deceived into thinking the stage was Rome in the first place — "the truth is, that the spectators are always in their senses." If the rules could not accommodate the best work, the rules were wrong.

The second was philosophical. German Romantic criticism, particularly Friedrich Schlegel and later Hegel, recast genres as historical rather than eternal. Genres were not fixed slots waiting to be filled but forms that emerged, developed and died in specific circumstances, each expressing the spirit of its age. Hegel's Aesthetics, delivered as lectures in the 1820s, organised the arts into symbolic, classical and romantic phases and the literary genres into a developmental sequence: epic representing the objective world, lyric the subjective interior, and drama the reconciliation of the two. Whatever one thinks of the metaphysics, this made genre history a serious subject.

The Romantics also elevated the lyric, which the classical hierarchy had ranked low, and elevated originality over conformity. Edward Young's Conjectures on Original Composition (1759) had already opposed original to imitative genius, and the Romantic critical vocabulary — spontaneity, sincerity, the individual voice — worked systematically against the idea of writing to a pattern. Benedetto Croce took this to its logical end in Aesthetic (1902), arguing that genre classifications are mere practical conveniences with no aesthetic reality, since every genuine work of art is an individual intuition and thus its own kind.

This is the point at which the modern tension appears. The Croce position is intuitively appealing to writers, who tend to experience genre as a limitation, and it is untenable in practice, because as an account of reading it is simply false — readers demonstrably use genre knowledge constantly. Later theorists have tried to preserve the insight while rejecting the conclusion, arguing that genres are real as historical conventions and as reading strategies even if they are not real as fixed essences.

The nineteenth century added another development that reshaped the field materially rather than theoretically: the rise of the novel, a form with no classical pedigree, no rules and enormous commercial success. Its arrival forced a reconsideration of what genre systems were for, because the most important literary form of the age had appeared entirely outside them.

sections.heading: Structuralism and the Attempt at a Systematic Poetics
sections.body:
The twentieth century's most ambitious genre theory came from Russian Formalism and its structuralist successors, which sought a science of literature analogous to linguistics: a description of the underlying system that generates the observable works.

Vladimir Propp's Morphology of the Folktale (1928, translated into English in 1958) is the landmark demonstration. Analysing a corpus of 100 Russian fairy tales, Propp argued that although the characters and settings vary endlessly, the functions — the acts of characters defined by their significance for the plot — are limited to 31, and always occur in the same order, though any given tale uses only a subset. The hero is dispatched, a prohibition is violated, the villain causes harm, the hero is tested, receives a magical agent, is transferred to the object of search, and so on to the wedding. Propp also reduced the cast to seven roles: villain, donor, helper, princess and her father, dispatcher, hero, false hero. The claim was not that these tales are similar but that they are transformations of a single structure.

Northrop Frye's Anatomy of Criticism (1957) attempted something grander: a total map of literature. Frye organised narrative into four mythoi corresponding to the seasons — comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn, irony and satire with winter — and proposed a theory of modes in which the hero's power relative to ours and to the environment declines historically from myth (superior in kind) through romance, high mimetic, low mimetic to irony (inferior to us). The scheme is dazzling, deeply learned and impossible to falsify, which is the standard objection to it.

Tzvetan Todorov's Introduction to the Fantastic (1970) is the most careful structuralist genre study and the one whose method best repays attention. He defines the fantastic not by content — ghosts, magic — but by a reader's hesitation. A text is fantastic while the reader cannot decide whether the strange events have a natural explanation or a supernatural one. Resolve toward natural explanation and the text becomes uncanny; resolve toward the supernatural and it becomes marvellous. The fantastic is therefore a knife-edge that most texts occupy only temporarily. This definition is genuinely productive: it explains why Henry James's The Turn of the Screw generates a century of unresolvable argument, and it predicts which texts will do so.

Todorov also drew the crucial distinction between theoretical genres, deduced from a system of possible combinations, and historical genres, observed in actual literary practice, and argued that the two rarely coincide. His other durable contribution is the observation that a new genre is always a transformation of one or several older ones, by inversion, displacement or combination — which supplies a mechanism for genre change rather than merely noting that it happens.

sections.heading: Family Resemblance, Prototypes and the Cognitive Turn
sections.body:
The structuralist project ran into a persistent problem: no genre survives an attempt to define it by necessary and sufficient conditions. Every proposed rule for what makes a novel, a tragedy or a detective story has counterexamples that competent readers nonetheless assign to the category without hesitation. Something was wrong with the model of categories being used.

The philosophical repair came from Ludwig Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations (1953), which examined the concept "game" and found no feature common to all games — not competition, not rules, not winning, not amusement — but rather "a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing," which he called family resemblance. Alastair Fowler applied this directly to literature in Kinds of Literature (1982), arguing that literary genres are constituted by repertoires of features from which individual works draw selectively, so that membership is a matter of resemblance to other members rather than possession of a defining trait. Fowler's related insight is that genres have life cycles: an early formative phase, a secondary phase of self-conscious elaboration, and a tertiary phase of parody, burlesque or symbolic use, after which the genre may die or be recombined.

The empirical repair came from cognitive psychology. Eleanor Rosch's work on categorisation in the 1970s demonstrated that people do not represent everyday categories by definitions but by prototypes — best examples — with membership graded rather than binary. A robin is judged a better example of "bird" than a penguin, and this shows up in reaction times, in listing order and in what people infer. Applied to genre, this predicts that readers will judge some novels more novel-like than others, that borderline cases will be genuinely borderline rather than merely undecided, and that categories will have fuzzy edges without therefore being useless. All three predictions hold.

This reframing dissolves a great deal of unproductive argument. The question "is Frankenstein science fiction?" has no yes-or-no answer because category membership is not that kind of property. What can be answered is which features it shares with the prototype, how central those features are, and what is gained or lost by reading it under that description.

Cognitive approaches have added further mechanisms. Schema theory holds that readers deploy stored knowledge structures — scripts for what happens at a restaurant, or in a haunted house — and that genre labels activate the relevant schema at the outset. Work on the psychology of expectation suggests that pleasure in genre fiction comes substantially from the interplay of prediction and mild violation, an account related to models of musical pleasure. There is also evidence that genre labelling changes evaluation directly: identical passages are rated differently when presented as literary fiction versus genre fiction, which is a measurable effect rather than a critical opinion.

sections.heading: How Genres Actually Form: Rhetoric, Situation and Convention
sections.body:
A separate and unusually powerful line of thinking asks not what genres are but where they come from, and answers that they arise from recurrent situations rather than from formal features.

Carolyn Miller's essay "Genre as Social Action" (1984) is the pivotal statement. Her argument is that a genre is defined by the social action it accomplishes, not by its shape. The eulogy is a genre because funerals recur and require something to be said; its formal features follow from that function. This inverts the usual analysis: form does not define the genre, the recurring rhetorical situation does, and form is what stabilises around it. The approach originated in rhetoric and composition studies but applies equally to literature.

The mechanism of stabilisation is worth spelling out because it explains both why genres are conventional and why they are not arbitrary. When a situation recurs, writers who face it look at how it was handled before, because starting from nothing is expensive and because readers who have seen previous instances have expectations. Successful solutions are copied. Over enough repetitions the copied solutions become normative, and eventually a writer who departs from them is understood as making a statement rather than merely writing differently. At that point a genre exists. Nothing about this process requires a legislator, which is why almost no genre has a founding document and why genre names are usually applied retrospectively, often by critics or booksellers rather than by the writers involved.

Mikhail Bakhtin's concept of speech genres, developed in an essay written around 1953, extends this to all language use. Every sphere of activity, he argued, develops its relatively stable types of utterance — the military command, the domestic greeting, the scientific paper — and we speak in these types as unavoidably as we speak in a language. Literary genres are secondary or complex speech genres that absorb and rework primary ones. Bakhtin's related and more famous claim concerns the novel, which he treated not as one genre among others but as an anti-genre: a form defined by heteroglossia, the incorporation of many social voices, and by its capacity to swallow other genres whole. In "Epic and Novel" he argued that epic addresses an absolute past sealed off from the present, while the novel operates in a zone of maximal contact with the unfinished present, which is why the novel can never be finished as a form.

The rhetorical account also explains genre change materially. When the situation changes, the genre changes or dies. The verse epistle declined with the postal and social conditions that sustained it. The three-volume Victorian novel died within about five years of Mudie's circulating library ceasing to buy them in 1894, a change driven not by aesthetics but by distribution economics. The sitcom's 22-minute length came from American advertising slots. Genres are shaped by their material conditions of production and circulation at least as much as by literary influence.

sections.heading: Mode, Form and Kind: Sorting Out the Vocabulary
sections.body:
Much confusion in genre discussion is caused by using one word for several different levels of classification, and a reader who separates them will find a large fraction of apparent disagreement dissolves.

The most useful distinction is between mode and kind. A kind, sometimes called a historical genre, is a specific, historically situated, formally identifiable type: the Petrarchan sonnet, the Gothic novel, the Restoration comedy, the hard-boiled detective story. Kinds have datable beginnings, characteristic features, canonical examples and often ends. A mode, by contrast, is an adjectival quality that can be applied across kinds and periods: the tragic, the comic, the pastoral, the elegiac, the satiric, the ironic. There are tragic novels, tragic films and tragic lyrics; tragedy as a kind is a specific dramatic form largely confined to certain periods. Fowler's rule of thumb is that kinds are nouns and modes are adjectives, and that when a kind dies its mode often survives and colonises other kinds — pastoral as a dramatic and poetic kind is largely gone, while the pastoral mode is everywhere.

A third level is form or external structure: the physical or formal shape independent of content. The sonnet, the sequence of fourteen lines, is a form; it has carried love complaint, political polemic, devotional meditation and comic insult. Verse, prose, dialogue, epistolary construction and first-person narration are formal choices that cut across both kind and mode.

A fourth level, particularly important in commercial contexts, is the category or marketing genre: romance, thriller, science fiction, horror, literary fiction. These are shelving decisions with real consequences for what gets published, reviewed, taught and read. They correlate imperfectly with any formal analysis. "Literary fiction" is the clearest case of a marketing category masquerading as an aesthetic one; it names a set of production and reception practices — reviewed in certain places, submitted for certain prizes, taught in certain courses — rather than a set of textual features, and defining it formally has defeated everyone who has tried.

A fifth consideration is the distinction between authorial and readerly genre. A text may be written in one kind and read in another, and the two need not agree. Robinson Crusoe was written and initially received as an authentic traveller's account; it is now read as a founding novel. Gulliver's Travels was written as satire and has been read for three centuries as a children's adventure. Neither reading is simply wrong; they are different contracts activated by different readers in different circumstances, and the history of a text's reception is often a history of its reclassification.

Keeping these five levels distinct makes it possible to say precisely what is being claimed. "Moby-Dick is not a novel" is unfalsifiable noise; "Moby-Dick draws on the formal conventions of the encyclopedic anatomy more than the domestic realist kind, in a predominantly tragic mode" is a claim that can be examined.

sections.heading: Genre Change, Hybridity and the Life of Forms
sections.body:
Genres are not stable, and the ways they change are systematic enough to describe.

The Russian Formalists supplied the first mechanical account. Viktor Shklovsky argued in 1917 that art works by defamiliarisation, making the familiar strange so that perception is renewed, and that any device loses its power through repetition. Genre change is therefore driven by the automatisation of conventions: what was once startling becomes invisible, and writers must escalate, invert or abandon it. Yuri Tynyanov added the idea of the literary system, in which genres compete for a dominant position, and of the periodic promotion of marginal forms to the centre — the "junior branch" displacing the exhausted senior line. This explains why novels absorbed the letter, the diary, the newspaper report and the case history at points when the established literary forms felt exhausted.

Parody is the most visible mechanism and often the most consequential. Don Quixote (1605, 1615) is a parody of chivalric romance that became the founding work of the European novel. Northanger Abbey parodies the Gothic. Fowler's tertiary phase in the life of a kind is typically parodic, and the parody frequently outlives what it mocks, which is why many readers know the parody of a form better than the form itself.

Hybridisation is the second major mechanism, and it is now so pervasive that pure examples of most kinds are hard to find. The historical novel fuses romance and chronicle. Magical realism, associated with Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) and with earlier work by Alejo Carpentier and Jorge Luis Borges, combines realist narration with unremarked supernatural event, and its defining feature is precisely the narrator's refusal to treat the marvellous as remarkable. Autofiction fuses memoir with novel and makes the boundary itself the subject. The nonfiction novel, announced by Truman Capote for In Cold Blood (1966), applies novelistic technique to documented fact.

Ralph Cohen argued influentially in 1986 that genres are "open categories" and that every new member changes the category itself — a text does not merely join a genre, it alters what the genre is. This is a strong claim with real evidence behind it: what "science fiction" names in 2020 is not what it named in 1940, and the change was produced by the works.

A fourth mechanism is technological and institutional. New media generate new genres and modify old ones. Serialisation in Victorian magazines produced the cliffhanger and the large cast. Cinema produced the shot-reverse-shot grammar that has fed back into prose. Digital publishing has enabled forms that could not previously be sustained, from very long serialised web fiction to interactive narrative, and platform recommendation systems have created micro-genres with names — cosy fantasy, litRPG, grimdark — that arose in reader communities and were adopted by publishers afterward.

sections.heading: The Major Prose Kinds and Their Distinctive Machinery
sections.body:
Individual kinds have characteristic engines, and describing them concretely is more useful than listing conventions.

Detective fiction is the most formally analysed of popular kinds because its constraints are the most explicit. The classical or "golden age" puzzle story runs on a strict information contract: the reader must in principle be able to solve the crime, which requires that every clue given to the detective be given to the reader. Ronald Knox's "Ten Commandments" of 1929 and S. S. Van Dine's twenty rules of 1928 codified this, banning identical twins, unknown poisons, supernatural agency and the detective as culprit. The hard-boiled variant developed by Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler abandoned the puzzle contract in favour of atmosphere and moral compromise; Chandler's essay "The Simple Art of Murder" (1944) is an explicit attack on the puzzle school as artificial. Structurally, Todorov observed that the whodunnit contains two stories — the crime and the investigation — with the first told through the second, which is why the form is so amenable to formal experiment.

Science fiction's distinctive device is what Darko Suvin, in Metamorphoses of Science Fiction (1979), called the novum: a single strange innovation, rationally explicable within the story's frame, from which consequences are extrapolated. Suvin defined the genre by "cognitive estrangement," combining the estrangement of fantasy with a cognitive, rule-governed logic. The definition is contested — it excludes much that readers call science fiction and smuggles in an evaluative preference — but it identifies the mechanism accurately. Samuel Delany's related point is that science fiction requires a distinct reading protocol: the sentence "her world exploded" is figurative in realist fiction and possibly literal here, and competent readers hold both readings open.

Romance, the largest-selling prose category by a wide margin, is defined by Pamela Regis in A Natural History of the Romance Novel (2003) through eight narrative elements and one absolute requirement, the emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending. That guarantee is not a weakness in the form but its organising principle: because the outcome is assured, the interest lies wholly in the obstacle and its overcoming, in the same way that the guaranteed solution organises a detective story.

Horror is defined by affect rather than content, which makes it a mode as much as a kind. Noël Carroll's The Philosophy of Horror (1990) analyses "art-horror" as a compound of fear and disgust directed at a monster that is both threatening and impure — categorically interstitial, violating the boundaries between living and dead, human and animal, self and other. This explains the recurrence of certain monster types across unrelated cultures.

The realist novel's machinery is the least visible because it is the default, but it is no less conventional: free indirect discourse, the sustained illusion of unmediated access to consciousness, chronological plotting with causal linkage, and the assumption that individual psychology is the proper unit of explanation are all historically specific devices, developed largely between 1740 and 1880.

sections.heading: Poetic and Dramatic Kinds
sections.body:
Verse and drama classify along partly different axes from prose, and their genre systems are older and more formally explicit.

The classical division of poetry into epic, lyric and dramatic is usually attributed to Aristotle but is really a later construction, consolidated in the eighteenth century and given philosophical weight by Hegel and Goethe, who called them the three natural forms. Epic is long narrative verse on heroic action, typically opening in medias res with an invocation, using elevated diction, epic similes and catalogues; Homer, Virgil, and in English Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) are the reference points, and the mock-epic — Pope's The Rape of the Lock (1712) — is the parodic tertiary phase.

Lyric is the category that has expanded to absorb nearly all modern poetry, which creates its own problems. Originally meaning verse sung to the lyre, it came to mean short, non-narrative, subjective utterance in a single speaking voice. Its subdivisions are numerous and mostly defined by occasion or form: the ode (elevated address, Pindaric or Horatian), the elegy (lament for the dead, though in classical usage the term denoted a metre rather than a subject), the pastoral or eclogue (idealised rural dialogue), the aubade (dawn parting), the epithalamion (wedding), the epigram (short and pointed), the ballad (narrative in quatrains, originally oral and communal). Jonathan Culler's Theory of the Lyric (2015) argues that treating lyric as the dramatic monologue of a fictional speaker — the standard classroom approach since the New Critics — is a historical accident that misdescribes most of the tradition, in which the poem is an event of address rather than a representation of a person speaking.

Fixed forms classify by structure rather than subject. The sonnet's fourteen lines admit the Italian or Petrarchan division into octave and sestet with a turn at line nine, and the English or Shakespearean three quatrains and couplet with the turn often deferred to line thirteen. The villanelle's nineteen lines and two refrains, the sestina's six repeated end-words rotating through six stanzas and an envoi, the ghazal's independent couplets sharing a rhyme and refrain, the haiku's syllabic count and seasonal reference, all constrain in ways that generate rather than merely limit.

Dramatic kinds classify partly by outcome and partly by social level. Tragedy concerns elevated persons and ends in catastrophe; comedy concerns ordinary or low persons and ends in reconciliation, conventionally marriage. Between and around them proliferated tragicomedy, the problem play, the history play, the masque, the farce, melodrama with its music-cued moral absolutes, and the well-made play with its clockwork exposition and obligatory scene. Modern drama's characteristic move has been to refuse these categories: naturalism claimed to abolish the distinction of rank, absurdism refused resolution altogether, and Brecht's epic theatre attacked the emotional identification on which both tragic and comic effect had depended.

sections.heading: Nonfiction Kinds and the Boundary of the Literary
sections.body:
Genre theory long treated nonfiction as an afterthought, which is odd given that most reading in most periods has been nonfiction, and the neglect has left the categories less well analysed than they deserve.

The essay is the central literary nonfiction kind and was effectively invented as such by Michel de Montaigne, whose Essais appeared from 1580. His title means attempts or trials, and the form's defining feature is the visible movement of a mind working on a subject without arriving at system. Francis Bacon's Essays (1597) established a drier, more aphoristic English variant. The distinction between the familiar or personal essay and the formal or expository essay dates from this fork, and modern subdivisions — the lyric essay, the critical essay, the polemic, the review — all descend from it.

Biography and autobiography raise the sharpest theoretical questions because they make truth claims about persons. Philippe Lejeune's concept of the autobiographical pact (1975) is the key analytic tool: autobiography is defined not by internal features, which it shares with the novel, but by an identity contract between the names of author, narrator and protagonist, signalled outside the text on the title page. This is why a novel written in convincing confessional first person is not autobiography and why the discovery that a memoir was fabricated changes the text's status without changing a word of it. Memoir differs from autobiography chiefly in scope, treating a period or theme rather than a life.

History writing has its own long-running dispute about whether it is a literary genre. Hayden White's Metahistory (1973) argued that historians emplot their material using the same narrative structures as fiction — romance, tragedy, comedy, satire — and that this "emplotment" is a choice not determined by the evidence. The strong version of the claim, that historical narrative is a form of fiction-making, has been resisted vigorously by working historians who point out that evidence constrains what can be said, and the resulting argument about the limits of narrativism is unresolved and worth taking seriously in both directions.

Travel writing, nature writing, science writing, the sermon, the pamphlet, the manifesto, the letter and the diary all have describable conventions and histories. The diary is particularly interesting because its convention is the absence of an addressee, which is a fiction — diarists overwhelmingly write with imagined readers — and because publication converts it into a different kind entirely.

The boundary question that runs under all of this is whether "literature" is itself a genre. Since roughly the eighteenth century it has named a value category rather than a descriptive one, and attempts to define it by formal features — fictionality, self-referential language, deviation from ordinary usage — have all failed against counterexamples. The more defensible position, argued by Terry Eagleton among others, is that literature names a way of being read and institutionally treated rather than a property of texts.

sections.heading: Genre, Value and the Hierarchy Problem
sections.body:
Genre classification has never been neutral. From the classical hierarchy that ranked epic above pastoral to the modern bookshop that separates "fiction" from "science fiction," sorting texts has been inseparable from ranking them, and the rankings have consequences for what is published, preserved, taught and studied.

The modern version of the hierarchy took shape in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries alongside the professionalisation of literary study and the expansion of mass-market publishing. The distinction between highbrow and lowbrow — the terms are borrowed from discredited phrenology and entered common use around 1900 — mapped onto a distinction between the difficult and the popular, and modernist aesthetics reinforced it by treating accessibility as suspect. Q. D. Leavis's Fiction and the Reading Public (1932) is a representative document, treating popular fiction as a social problem. Genre fiction became the residual category: what was left when literature had been removed.

Several arguments have been made against the hierarchy, with differing degrees of force. The historical argument observes that today's classics were frequently yesterday's genre products — Elizabethan drama was commercial entertainment, Dickens was serialised popular fiction, film noir was B-picture filler — and that the sorting is therefore unreliable as a judgement of durability. The empirical argument observes that the formal features supposedly distinguishing literary from genre writing do not survive examination, since experimental technique appears throughout popular forms and conventional plotting appears throughout prestigious ones. The sociological argument, developed most rigorously by Pierre Bourdieu in Distinction (1979) and The Rules of Art (1992), analyses taste as a marker of class position and the literary field as a structure in which "disinterested" art accrues symbolic capital precisely by disavowing commercial success.

None of these arguments establishes that all texts are equally good, and it is worth being clear about that, because the debate is frequently conducted as though the only options were a rigid hierarchy and a refusal to evaluate. What they establish is narrower: that the genre label is a poor proxy for quality, that the assignment of labels is a social process with identifiable interests behind it, and that judgements made at the level of the category rather than the work are unreliable.

The practical effects are measurable. Studies of review coverage consistently show that works marketed as genre fiction receive a small fraction of the review attention given to comparable literary fiction. Prize eligibility often excludes categories outright. Academic study of popular forms was marginal until the growth of cultural studies from the 1960s and remains uneven. Authors respond strategically: the phenomenon of literary novelists writing science fiction while denying that it is science fiction, and the counter-phenomenon of genre writers claiming literary standing, are both intelligible as moves within a field where the label carries material stakes.

sections.heading: Genre in Practice: Publishing, Libraries and Algorithms
sections.body:
Outside criticism, genre is an operational system with rules, staff and money behind it, and the practical classifications diverge from the theoretical ones in instructive ways.

Publishing uses genre to manage risk. A category with an established readership has a predictable sales floor, which determines advance size, print run, cover design, retail placement and marketing spend. This produces a strong pressure toward legibility: a manuscript that does not fit a category is harder to sell because no one knows where to shelve it or whom to sell it to. The commonest practical advice given to new novelists — know your genre and your comparable titles — is a description of this machinery rather than an aesthetic doctrine. It also produces recognisable cover conventions, which function as genre signals doing work before a word is read: the metallic serif and spacecraft of science fiction, the clinch of category romance, the fogged street of the thriller.

Library and bibliographic classification is a separate system with different purposes. The Dewey Decimal Classification, devised by Melvil Dewey in 1876, and the Library of Congress Classification handle literature primarily by language and period rather than by kind, which reflects a scholarly rather than a readerly logic. Fiction is often shelved alphabetically by author with genre indicated by spine stickers, a workaround acknowledging that readers browse by kind while catalogues are organised by provenance. Bibliographic standards have moved toward explicit genre and form terms — the Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms vocabulary, developed from 2007, distinguishes what a work is from what it is about, a distinction earlier subject headings collapsed.

Algorithmic recommendation is now the dominant practical classifier for many readers and works on entirely different principles. Collaborative filtering does not analyse texts at all; it groups items by co-consumption, inferring that people who liked A also liked B. The categories this produces are behavioural rather than formal, and they are often finer-grained and stranger than any critical taxonomy. Netflix's several thousand "altgenres," generated by combining tags for tone, setting, era and character type, is the best-documented example. The consequences are double-edged: micro-genres let small audiences find work that no shelf would have carried, and recommendation loops can also narrow exposure and reward conformity to whatever the system has already identified as a cluster.

Self-publishing platforms have made category selection a direct commercial decision by the author, since the chosen category determines competition for visibility. This has produced rapid genre proliferation with names invented by writers and readers rather than publishers, and an unusually visible record of genre formation happening in real time — which is a genuine research opportunity, since most historical genre formation has to be reconstructed from fragmentary evidence.

sections.heading: Working With Genre: A Practical Method for Classifying a Text
sections.body:
Classifying a text well is a skill with a procedure, and it is worth setting out because the commonest errors come from skipping steps rather than from lacking knowledge. Readers who are confident about literature often produce poor classifications because they begin with a label they already have in mind and then search for evidence supporting it, which is the reverse of what works. The method below runs the other way: purpose first, then evidence, then comparison, then a label held loosely and stated with its uncertainty attached.

Two habits make the difference in practice. The first is separating description from judgement — noting that a text uses an unreliable narrator, a rural setting and a withheld revelation is description, while calling it a psychological thriller is already a judgement with consequences. The second is treating the classification as a hypothesis that predicts things, then checking those predictions.
steps: State why you are classifying. Shelving, teaching, reviewing, writing a marketing description and making a scholarly argument have different requirements, and a classification adequate for one may be useless for another. Most confused genre arguments are between people with different purposes who have not said so.

Separate the levels before assigning anything: external form (verse or prose, length, structural pattern), kind (the historically specific type), mode (the adjectival quality — tragic, comic, satiric), and market category. Assign each independently rather than collapsing them into a single label.

Identify the reading protocol the text asks for in its first two or three pages. Note what it expects you to accept without explanation, what it treats as remarkable, and what kind of question it invites. This is usually a faster and more reliable guide to kind than a features checklist.

List concrete conventional features actually present: characteristic figures, settings, plot movements, diction, narrative stance, opening and closing formulas. Work from the text rather than from the label already applied to it.

Compare against a prototype — a work you and your intended reader would both accept as a central example of the candidate genre — and describe the distance in specific terms rather than judging membership yes or no.

Check the historical fit. Ask whether the genre name existed when the text was written, and if not, what its contemporaries called it. Anachronistic labelling is legitimate but should be conscious, since calling Frankenstein science fiction imports a category invented in 1926.
Look for the hybrid seam. Most interesting texts combine kinds, and the point of contact is usually where the meaning is. Name both parents rather than forcing a single classification.
